notes.key_messages: When writing explanations, a sequence of short statements is often clearer that trying to convey ideas in unnecessarily long sentences. Candidates need to avoid giving an answer which is simply a restatement of the question. Candidates should be guided by the number of marks allocated to a question and also the amount of space provided, although it is not usually necessary to use all of the space. It is often beneficial for a candidate to read again through their answer to make sure that the meaning is clear. Some candidates would benefit from improving the way they lay out their working in numerical questions so that they can gain credit from it.
notes.general_comments: The questions on this paper allowed candidates of all abilities to show their strengths to maximum effect. Most of the numerical work required the knowledge of a formula, the substitution of data and a calculation of the final answer, with few complicating issues. On such questions the performance was particularly good, including a high proportion of those of lower overall ability. This means that weaker candidates have learnt and could recall important basic formulae. There is no reason why many of these candidates, with sufficient encouragement and motivation, should not also be able learn and recall definitions and meanings of physical terms and words, an area in which much of their under-performance lies. The parts of questions requiring verbal explanations and descriptions are areas where significant problems arise for candidates whose skills in English are limited. Sometimes in such questions candidates give the impression that they think they must fill the space available. They try to convey their ideas in unnecessarily long sentences when a sequence of short statements would suffice. It is likely that candidates are advised to read the whole of a question before setting out to write the answers to the separate parts. However, it is sometimes apparent that the initial reading introduces unnecessary ideas into a candidate’s mind, and leads to answers to the early parts of questions including points which are only relevant to later sections of the question. They should be reminded that they can answer early parts of questions on the basis of what they have read so far and the learning they have achieved in the topic concerned. With few exceptions, candidates wrote answers to all the questions, suggesting that teachers had managed to achieve comprehensive coverage of the syllabus, for which great credit is due. Also it was encouraging to note that very few errors over units were made in this paper, and more often by omission than by writing down the wrong one.
notes.1a: Sound knowledge of the classification of quantities as scalars or vectors was generally evident. The quantity most often wrongly classified was kinetic energy.
notes.1bi: This was almost invariably answered correctly, as was (ii).
notes.1biii: Most candidates identified friction or air resistance as a slowing factor. A small minority suggested the idea that the force or acceleration provided by the kick persists after the ball loses contact with the foot.
notes.1biv: Candidates had been told that the average speeds between A and B and between B and C were the same, and had to remember that velocity is a vector quantity. A minority of candidates missed one or other of these points.
notes.2a: Most candidates correctly quoted kinetic energy, heat/thermal/y internal energy, and sound energy. Strain energy was rejected on the basis that this was gained by the belt as a consequence of loss of potential energy by the package.
notes.2b: The vast majority quoted mgh, and arrived at the correct answer with the right unit.
notes.2c: Most were successful. A few wrote down P = W/t and calculated a different value for W than had been calculated in (b).
notes.2d: Three points were required, each for a mark. Most candidates gained credit for saying the speed of the belt was lower or that it took a longer time to raise the package. Many also referred to the greater increase in P.E. of the package or of the need for the motor to do more work. Fewer made the connection between power, work and time by quoting t = W/P or the equivalent.
notes.3a: A large majority did not include all the necessary detail. ‘Force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the point’ was required. The words ‘perpendicular’ and ‘from the point’ were usually missed.
notes.3bi: A downward pointing arrow at the centre of the bar was usually drawn, but surprisingly many placed the arrow at the pivot or the right-hand end of the bar. Some showed the arrow in the correct place but pointing upwards.
notes.3bii: Many did not use the given dimensions correctly to calculate the distance.
notes.3biii: The fact that the question used the words ‘total’ and ‘forces’ should have suggested to candidates that more than one moment was involved. However, the great majority did not include the moment due to the weight of the bar.
notes.3biv: With the benefit of any error from (iii) carried forward, full credit was usually awarded.
notes.3bv: Either by analysing the previous numerical work, or by knowing how a crowbar works, many candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.4a: This question effectively asked for a definition of specific latent heat of fusion. Unfortunately, a majority of candidates did not include the words ‘at constant temperature’, ‘at 0 C’ or ‘at freezing point’.
notes.4bi: Most candidates clearly understood the information conveyed by the graph, but some did not take note of the words ‘what is taking place’ and wrote freezing or melting point, instead of ice melting, for B to C, and boiling point instead of water boiling for D to E. The word evaporating was not rewarded.
notes.4bii: Correct comparisons of the latent heat values were usually made and credit awarded.
notes.4biii: Fewer made the correct comparison of the specific heat capacities but those who did were awarded credit. For further credit, a sensible reference to the reason for the different slopes of AB and CD had to be made.
notes.5ai: Two of the following points about molecules were required to gain credit: random motion, high speed, collision with each other or the container walls. Only the random motion aspect was quoted in many cases. The provision of three answer lines should have keyed candidates into providing more than a one word answer.
notes.5aii: The only point required here was ‘molecules hit the walls’ expressed in some way. A number of candidates wrote statements like ‘molecules move faster and hit the walls harder’ seeming to anticipate, albeit wrongly, aspects of the question following in (b).
notes.5aiii: A very large majority of the candidates calculated the force correctly.
notes.5bi: Almost all candidates arrived at the correct answer. Many candidates wrote down an expression of Boyle’s law and substituted the correct values. Others simply saw that the volume was halved, applied Boyle’s law mentally, and wrote down the correct answer. Candidates are advised to show their working, however, since credit can be given for correct working even in the final answer is incorrect.
notes.5bii: The answer required a mention of collision of molecules with the walls and that these collisions occurred with greater frequency, or words to that effect. Omission of the reference to frequency suggested incomplete understanding of the ideas, so no credit was awarded. A substantial number of candidates implied that increase of pressure leads to an increase in the speed of the molecules.
notes.6ai: Candidates needed to suggest in their answer that the free end of the rope had to be moved repetitively. Most answers succeeded in this requirement.
notes.6aii: Most candidates know a definition of wavelength and attempted to show the distance on the figure. Many were successful, but some of the attempts to indicate its length on the figure were less precise than required. A majority did not know the meaning of amplitude and labelled the peak-to-peak distance.
notes.6aiii: Most answers conveyed in some way that the rate of moving the rope, compared with the answer to (i), had to be increased, thus showing their awareness that a reduction in wavelength required an increase in frequency.
notes.6b: A complete answer needed recognition of the reduced wavelength in the shallower water, the fact that the frequency is constant, and a statement of the relationship between speed, wavelength and frequency. A commendable number made the appropriate points and achieved full credit. The factor most often missed was the constant nature of the frequency. Those who stated that speed is proportional to wavelength also had to mention the constant frequency in order to make sense of the proportionality.
notes.7a: The fact that the focal length is the distance between a principal focus or focal point and the centre of the lens, or simply the lens, is not well known. Many took no note of the word ‘length’ and wrote about a point instead.
notes.7bi: Many misconceptions were apparent in the candidates’ ideas about a real image. Acceptable answers referred to an image which can be formed on a screen or other surface or an image formed by rays of light meeting. The answer ‘not virtual’, often quoted, was not accepted.
notes.7bii: The rays drawn had to start at A and finish, or pass through, B. Most candidates were correct in drawing ray 1 as a straight line from A to B, but many of these did not place the lens line at the intersection of this the ray and the principal axis. Some of those who drew ray 2 correctly did not show F, the principal focus, at the appropriate point. Ray 3 posed a problem for many, with some not showing it at all; any ray starting at A, bending at the lens and passing through B would suffice.
notes.7biii: There were three choices for each answer: smaller, larger or the same. Those who gained full credit probably worked out their answers by applying knowledge of ray diagrams.
notes.8a: Candidates have no doubt been taught that the term electromotive force is misleading, but many of them continue to describe the quantity as the force which drives a current. An acceptable meaning at this level is given in the syllabus: i.e. the energy supplied by a source (1 marking point) in driving charge round a complete circuit (1 marking point). The acceptable alternative was ‘the voltage or p.d. across a source (1 marking point) when not connected to a circuit (1 marking point). Some variation in the wording was allowed in either case.
notes.8b: In (i) and (ii) the answers were almost invariably correct.
notes.8c: This was a testing question making demands on the thought processes of even the most able candidates. Most of those who did tackle the problem calculated the current in the circuit with the lamps in series, arrived at a value for the current just below the normal operating current of both bulbs, and drew the correct conclusion. The alternative approach, used by a few who knew the appropriate formula, was to calculate the p.d. across each lamp, showing that these were just below the normal operating p.d. of both bulbs.
notes.9ai: The rule was applied correctly in the majority of cases.
notes.9aii: The question effectively told candidates that a current in a wire placed in a magnetic field experiences a force, so an answer repeating this idea was not acceptable, nor was an answer stating that Fleming’s left-hand rule applies. A more fundamental reason was required, such as expressing the idea that the current produces a magnetic field, which interacts with that of the magnet to cause the force.
notes.9aiii: Only answers suggesting reversal of the direction in (i) were accepted.
notes.9bi: Many candidates drew a curved line with an arrow, suggesting that the force acting was changing direction. These answers were rejected. Only an arrow at P pointing downwards, suggesting proper understanding of the rule in this case, was awarded credit.
notes.9bii: Credit was given for a suggestion that the particle followed a curved path, irrespective of the previous answer.
notes.10a: Most candidates drew an acceptable symbol for the OR gate. Those with a straight line at the input end or showing a triangular shape for the gate were rejected.
notes.10b: A large majority conveyed the correct information, with many completing a truth table to do so.
notes.10c: It was not intended that candidates should effectively repeat the answer to (b). Candidates needed to describe in some way the necessary features built into the car to provide the required signal. A good answer referred to the following: switches or sensors of some kind to respond to the opening or closing of the doors, connections from these switches to provide inputs to the gate, the output of the gate connected to some kind of alarm and giving a signal to the driver. Complete answers were rare.
notes.11ai: Most candidates could identify the proton as having a positive charge.
notes.11aii: All the possible pairings of the three particles were quoted, with rather more choosing the correct than either of the other possibilities.
notes.11b: A very large majority of candidates knew the meanings of the numbers preceding the symbol of the element and could do the arithmetic.
notes.11ci: Precise knowledge of the meaning of half-life and careful use of the graph was required. The lack of one or other of these requirements meant that many errors were made. Those with no real idea wrote down a count rate rather than a time.
notes.11cii: It was possible to gain full credit for any half-life value quoted in (i), with the error carried forward. However, it tended to be those with the correct value or one very close to 8 hours who were successful.
